title: Growth in a Time of Debt

original_source.central_claim: a marked debt–growth nonlinearity near public debt of 90% of GDP across advanced and emerging economies

source_manifest.title: Growth in a Time of Debt
source_manifest.finding: Historical descriptive analysis associates debt above 90% of GDP with markedly lower growth; it does not establish causation.

source_manifest.title: Does High Public Debt Consistently Stifle Economic Growth? A Critique of Reinhart and Rogoff
source_manifest.finding: Replication corrects spreadsheet errors, exclusions and weighting. The high-debt mean becomes 2.2%, not -0.1%; a consistent 90% discontinuity is rejected.

source_manifest.title: Debt and Growth: Is There a Magic Threshold?
source_manifest.finding: Longer horizons and debt trajectories undermine a unique growth cliff. The study supplements IMF data with data from the target paper and compares its empirical pattern.

source_manifest.title: Testing for a Debt-Threshold Effect on Output Growth
source_manifest.finding: Formal threshold estimation uses the Reinhart–Rogoff data; it finds no 90% threshold and explores a lower threshold with robustness qualifications.

source_manifest.title: The impact of high and growing government debt on economic growth: an empirical investigation for the euro area
source_manifest.finding: An independent panel study of twelve euro-area countries finds an inverted-U turning point near 90–100% under its model; this is bounded support, not validation of a universal cliff.

answers.rationale: The later euro-area study supports high-debt nonlinearity near the reported range within its twelve-country panel; contrary findings prevent treating this as consensus.
The direct replication does not recover the central dramatic high-debt result after correcting the analysis.

evidence.explanation: The reconstructed spreadsheet exposes the numerical and weighting dependence.

answers.rationale: The broad threshold does not survive tests of subsequent growth over longer horizons and debt trajectories.

evidence.explanation: Independent robustness tests reject a unique growth cliff.

answers.rationale: The later IMF assessment rejects a unique high-debt threshold, while allowing weaker debt–growth associations.

evidence.explanation: The central threshold interpretation is not retained.

search_gaps: Original six-page AER paper read; follow-up scopes are recorded individually. The 2017 source was intermittently inaccessible beyond the abstract and selected sections.

No verified official policy implementation artifact; political attention is not counted as demonstrated benefit. Later reuse of shared historical data does not credit this paper with creating every underlying series.
Some source dates resolve only to a publication year. Non-threshold findings about emerging-market external debt and inflation were not independently reassessed in equal depth.
Lifetime observation through 2026-09-16; the assigned pilot sample is not an unbiased estimate of all research outcomes.
research.summary: Bounded supportive evidence exists, but the striking 90% threshold fails direct correction and stronger tests. The paper remains a substantive empirical baseline; research uptake is not proof that its policy interpretation is valid.
